This surah was revealed concerning the Battle of Badr and its spoils. ﴿They ask you about the spoils of war.﴾ The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and those who asked were the Companions. Al-anfal means the spoils (al-ghanaʾim). On the day of Badr they were three groups: a group with the Prophet ﷺ in the ʿarish (a shelter) guarding him; a group that pursued the polytheists, killing and capturing them; and a group that gathered up the enemy's booty and baggage when they fled. When the fighting ended and the people came together, each group saw that it had more right to the spoil than the others, and they disagreed among themselves. So the verse was revealed. Its meaning: they ask you about the ruling on the spoils and who is entitled to them. It was also said: al-anfal here refers to what the leader (al-imam) grants (yunaffilu) to some of the army from the spoils in addition to their share. The jurists differed over whether this granting comes from the one-fifth (al-khums), which is the view of Malik, or from the four-fifths, or from the total of the spoils before the one-fifth is taken out.

﴿Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger.﴾ That is, the ruling concerning them belongs to God and the Messenger, not to you.

﴿And set right what is between you﴾ — that is, agree and be reconciled, and do not dispute. Here "dhat" means "the states" (al-ahwal), as stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is intended in this place to mean the very thing and its reality. Al-Zubayri said: the use of "dhat" to mean the very thing and its reality is not part of the Arabic language.

﴿And obey God and His Messenger﴾ — meaning, in the ruling concerning the spoils. ʿUbada ibn al-Samit said: "This was revealed about us, the people of Badr, when we disagreed and our characters deteriorated, so God took the spoils out of our hands and gave them to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who divided them equally. In that lay the fear of God, obedience to His Messenger, and setting right what is between us."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verses 2–4:

﴿Only the believers are﴾ — i.e., those whose faith is complete. Here "innama" (only) is for emphasis, intensification and restriction. ﴿Whose hearts tremble [when Allah is mentioned]﴾ — i.e., they fear. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verses 5–6:

﴿As your Lord brought you forth﴾ There are three interpretations of this.

The first: the kaf (ك, "like/as") may be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose sense is: "This situation is like the situation of your going forth"; that is, their state in disliking the distribution of the spoils is like their state when you went out to the battle. The second: the kaf may be in the accusative position, as an adjective to the verbal noun of the verb implied in His words, "The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger," meaning: the spoils were settled for Allah and the Messenger in a settlement like the settlement of your going forth. The third: the kaf is connected to His words "they argue with you," meaning: [they argue with you] "from your house" (min baytika), that is, your dwelling in Medina, when Allah brought you forth for the battle of Badr. ﴿And indeed, a party of the believers were averse﴾, meaning they disliked fighting the enemy. This is because the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria carrying great wealth, with forty riders accompanying it. Gabriel informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, so he set out with the Muslims. The people of Mecca heard of this, gathered, and went out in great numbers to protect their caravan. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said: "O Muhammad, Allah has promised you one of the two groups: either the caravan or Quraysh." The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions, and they said: "The caravan is more beloved to us than meeting the enemy." He said: "The caravan has already passed along the coast of the sea, and this is Abu Jahl, who has approached." Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said to him: "Proceed as you wish, for we will follow you." Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "By Him who sent you with the truth, if you were to plunge into this sea, we would plunge with you. So march with us in the blessing of Allah." ﴿They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become clear﴾: their argument concerned meeting Quraysh, by preferring to meet the caravan, since it had more wealth and fewer men. The clarity of the truth is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informing them that they would be victorious. ﴿As if they were being driven toward death﴾: a simile for their state in the extreme of their dread of meeting Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verses 9–10:

﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾: *idh* is a *badal* (substitute, or appositional element) for *idh* in ﴿when He promised you﴾. It is also said that it is connected to His statement ﴿so that He might establish the truth﴾, or to a suppressed verb. *Istighathatuhum* (their seeking help) means their supplication for aid and victory. ﴿Reinforcing you﴾: *mumiddukum*, that is, increasing your numbers. ﴿In successive ranks﴾: *murdifin*, from your saying *radafahu* when he followed him, and *ardaftuhu iyyahu* when I caused him to follow him. The meaning is that some of them follow others. Whoever reads it with a fatha on the *dal*, *murdafin*, it is a passive participle (*ism maf'ul*). Whoever reads it with a kasra, *murdifin*, it is an active participle (*ism fa'il*). Both readings are sound in meaning, because the angels who were sent down follow one another, so some of them are followers and some are followed. ﴿And Allah did not make it﴾: the pronoun refers to the promise, or to the reinforcement by angels.

﴿When He covered you with drowsiness﴾. The word إذ (idh, "when") is a substitute (badal) for the إذ in إذ يعدكم (idh yaʿiduukum, "when He promised you"). Alternatively, it is in the accusative as an object of النصر (al-nasr, "the victory"), or of what is meant by the victory from God, or it is governed by a suppressed verb whose implied sense is: remember. Whoever reads يغشيكم (yughashshikum) with a dammed yāʾ and without shaddah is using the form from أغشى (aghshā). Whoever reads it with a dammed yāʾ and with shaddah is using the form from غشّى (ghashshā) with shaddah. Both forms are transitive to two objects, so النعاس (al-nuʿās, "the drowsiness") is the object and the second object. The meaning is that He covers you with it, and this is a metaphor (istiʿārah) from ghishāʾ (covering). Whoever reads it with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and the shīn is using the form from غشي (ghashiya), which is transitive to one object, meaning: the drowsiness descends upon you. ﴿as a security from Him﴾. That is, as security (amanan). The pronoun in منه (minhu) refers to God, Exalted is He. أمنةً (amanatan) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). Ibn Mas'ud said: drowsiness at the onset of battle is a sign of safety from the enemy. ﴿and sends down upon you water from the sky﴾. This is an enumeration of another blessing. They lacked water during the Battle of Badr before they reached Badr, and it was said that this was after they arrived. So God sent down rain for them until the valleys flowed. ﴿to purify you thereby﴾. Some of them had become ritually impure (junub) and purified themselves with the rainwater, and the rest performed ablution (wuḍūʾ) with it. Before this they had no water for purification or for ablution. ﴿and to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾. So God sent down the rain and removed from them the whispering of Satan. ﴿and to strengthen your hearts﴾. That is, to make them firm by removing what Satan had whispered to them, and by energizing them and removing laziness from them. ﴿and make your feet firm thereby﴾. The pronoun in به (bihi) refers to the water. They were on a soft, sandy ground in which no foot could be firmly set. When the rain fell, the sand became compacted and the path hardened, making walking and standing easy on it. It is also narrated that this same rain made the path difficult for the polytheists, and thus it became clear that this was from the subtle kindness (luṭf) of God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verse 12–14:

﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you, so make firm those who believe"﴾ may be a substitution (badal) for the earlier ﴿when﴾ (idh), just as that earlier one is a substitution for the one before it; or the element governing it (al-'amil fihi) is "yuthbit" (He confirms).

﴿So make firm those who believe﴾ may mean that the confirmation is by the angels fighting alongside the believers, or by words of comfort and encouragement, which they spoke when they appeared in the forms of the sons of Adam, or by casting security into the hearts of the believers.

﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ may be part of God's address to the angels concerning the battle of Badr, completing the confirmation of the believers; or it may be a new statement about what God will do in the future.

﴿So strike above the necks﴾ may also be an address to the angels or to the believers. The meaning of "above the necks" (fawq al-a'naq) is "upon the necks" (ala al-a'naq), at the joint between the head and the neck, since that is the place of slaughter; a blow there severs the head. It was also said that what is meant is the heads, since they are above the necks, and it was said that what is meant is the necks and that "fawq" is superfluous (za'ida).

﴿Every fingertip﴾ — it was said that these are the joints (al-mafasil), and it was said that they are the fingers, which is the most well-known usage in the language. The benefit of this is that when a fighter's fingers are struck he is rendered unable to fight, so he can be captured or killed.

﴿That is because they opposed God and His Messenger﴾ — the reference is to what befell the disbelievers on the Day of Badr. The "ba'" (bi-anna) is causal (lil-ta'lil). "Shaqqu" derives from "shiqaq," which means enmity and separation.

﴿That, so taste it﴾ — the address here is to the disbelievers. "Dhalikum" is in the nominative case, its implied meaning being "that is the punishment or the torment." It may also be in the accusative, governed by "fadhuquhu" (so taste it), as in your saying: "Zaydan, so strike him."

﴿And that for the disbelievers﴾ — it is conjoined (atf) to "dhalik" under the assumption that it is nominative, or accusative, or as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), with the waw meaning "with."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verse 15–16:

﴿Zahfan﴾ (advancing in massed ranks) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "those who disbelieve" or from the subject of "you meet" (laqītum). Its meaning is facing one another in rows and persons, and the root of zaḥf is pushing forward. ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ is a prohibition of fleeing, restricted to the condition that the disbelievers are more than twice the number of the Muslims, as will be mentioned in its place. ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ i.e. the day of encounter, in any era, ﴿unless he is maneuvering for battle﴾ this is the charge after the retreat, so that he shows his enemy that he has been defeated, and then turns back upon him, and that is a form of deception in war. ﴿Or retiring to a company﴾ i.e. withdrawing to a group of Muslims. If the group is present in the battle, then retiring to it is permissible by consensus. The scholars differed concerning retiring to Medina, and to the Imam and the main body when none of these is present. It is narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that he said: "I am a company for every Muslim," and this is a permission for that. Fleeing from the major sins is also (implied). The phrase "maneuvering" (mutaḥarrifan) is in the accusative as an exception from the phrase "and whoever turns his back to them." Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), and "illā" is superfluous. The pattern of mutaḥayyiz is mutafayyil, and if it were on the pattern mutafaʿʿal it would have been mutaḥawwiz, since it derives from ḥāza yaḥūzu.

﴿So you did not kill them﴾ That is, it was not within your power to kill them, because they were more numerous than you and stronger; rather, Allah killed them through your support against them and through the angels. ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had taken a handful of dust and pebbles on the day of Badr and thrown them at the faces of the disbelievers, and they fled. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verse 19–23:

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verses 24–27:

﴿to that which gives you life﴾: i.e., to obedience. It was also said: to jihad, because one lives through victory.

﴿Do not betray Allah﴾: it was revealed concerning the story of Abu Lubabah, when he signaled to the Banu Qurayzah that the only thing awaiting them from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slaughter. It was also said: the meaning is, do not betray by misappropriating the spoils, though the wording is general.

﴿and betray your trusts﴾: it is coordinated with "do not betray," or it is in the accusative case.

This was said by al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, or by the rest of Quraysh, when they denied the Prophet (ﷺ). They called down curses upon themselves if his message was the truth. The sound report, however, is that it was Abu Jahl who said this, as narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two books. The word *al-haqq* (the truth) is in the accusative because it is the predicate of *kana* (was).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of their words is denial. That is: "If this is the truth, then punish us for rejecting it, but it is not the truth, so we do not deserve punishment." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verse 41:

﴿And know that whatever you obtain of any spoil﴾ Its wording is general, but what is intended is particular, because the wealth taken from the disbelievers is of different kinds. Some of it is subject to the khums (one-fifth levy): that which is taken by force after fighting. Some of it is not subject to the khums but belongs entirely to the one who took it: that which a person takes in enemy lands without any galloping of horses or riding of camels (ghayr ijaf), and that which the enemy abandons out of fear of drowning. Some of it belongs entirely to the imam (ruler), who takes from it what he needs and spends the rest on the public interests of the Muslims, and this is the fay' (property gained without fighting) over which no horses or riding camels were driven. ﴿Then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾ (the verse continues). Scholars differed over the division of the khums among these categories. One group said: it is spent in six shares: a share for Allah, for the upkeep of the Ka'bah; a share for the Prophet (ﷺ), for the public interests of the Muslims, and it was said: for the ruler after him; a share for the near kin (dhu al-qurba) who are not permitted to receive charity; a share for orphans; a share for the needy; and a share for the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil).

Al-Shafi'i said: it is divided into five shares, and no separate share is given to Allah. Mention of Allah first was only because, in his view, everything belongs to Him. Abu Hanifah said: it is divided into three shares: for orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. Malik said: the khums is left to the discretion (ijtihad) of the imam, who takes what suffices him and spends the rest on the public interests.

﴿If you have believed in Allah﴾ refers back to what came before. The meaning is: if you are believers, then know what Allah has stated to you concerning the division of the khums, act accordingly, and do not oppose it.

﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant﴾ means the Prophet (ﷺ), and what was sent down to him of the Qur'an and of victory. ﴿On the day of the criterion (yawm al-furqan)﴾ i.e., the day of distinction between truth and falsehood, which is the day of Badr. ﴿The day the two hosts met﴾ means the Muslims and the disbelievers.

It has been read with both a ḍamma and a kasra, and both are dialectal forms (lughatān). "Al-Dunyā" means the nearer one, close to Madina, and "al-Quṣwā" means the farther one, distant from it. ﴿وَٱلرَّكْبُ أَسْفَلَ مِنكُمْ﴾ means the caravan (al-'Ir) in which Abu Sufyan was, and he had swerved away from the road out of fear of the Prophet (ﷺ). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 8, verses 49–55:

﴿The hypocrites say﴾: those who were in Medina. It is also said: those who were with the disbelievers, a group of Quraysh including Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughira, al-Harith ibn Rabi'a ibn al-Aswad, Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Umayya ibn al-Hajjaj. Its implied meaning is: "and they say to them, 'Taste!'" The omitted speech, which is its object, is coordinated with "they strike." It is possible that what follows is also the speech of the angels, or that it is a new sentence. ﴿That is because Allah﴾: its implied meaning, according to Sibawayh (the grammarian), is "the matter is that." The bā' is causal, and the meaning is: Allah does not change a blessing He has bestowed upon His servants until they change what is in themselves by disbelief and disobedience. ﴿Like the custom of﴾: this was mentioned in Aal 'Imran.

﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives [of war] until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land.﴾ When the captives were taken on the day of Badr, Abu Bakr advised that they be spared, while Umar advised that they be killed. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 8, verses 71–75:

﴿And if they intend to betray you﴾ — the verse is a threat to them. ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ through to the end of the surah: its purpose is to explain the ranks of the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar), and of those who believed but did not emigrate until after al-Hudaybiyah. He began first with the Emigrants, then mentioned the Helpers, who sheltered and supported them, and he established the wilaya (guardianship, close alliance) among them, namely the wilaya of mutual cooperation, which was then abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And blood relatives are more entitled to one another﴾. ﴿And if they seek your help﴾ — since He negated wilaya and mutual support between the believers, it was said: this is the wilaya of inheritance between those who emigrated and the believers who did not emigrate. He commanded that they be supported if they sought help from the believers, except if they sought help against a people with whom the believers have a covenant, in which case they must not support them against them. ﴿Unless you do it, there will be discord on earth﴾ — "illa" here is compounded of the conditional "in" and the negative "la". The pronoun in "taf'aluhu" refers either to the guardianship and mutual support of the believers, or to the keeping of the covenant mentioned in His saying: "except against a people between whom and you there is a covenant," or to the support mentioned in His saying: "then you must give support." The meaning: if you do not do that, there will be discord. ﴿And those who believed and emigrated﴾ — the verse is praise of the Emigrants and the Helpers and a promise to them, and "generous provision" refers to Paradise. ﴿And those who believed afterward﴾ — meaning those who emigrated after al-Hudaybiyah and the Pledge of al-Ridwan. ﴿And blood relatives are more entitled to one another﴾ — it was said: it abrogates inheritance between the Emigrants and the Helpers. Malik said: it does not concern inheritance. Abu Hanifa said: it concerns inheritance, and by it he required the inheritance of the maternal uncle, the paternal aunt, and other dhawu al-arham (blood relatives). ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an; and it was said: the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).
